paras: The attempted lynching of Johnson Reed was a gathering of crowds near the county jail at Pikeville, Kentucky, on a Sunday night in February 1903, with the aim of hanging Reed, a Black prisoner charged with assaulting a white girl. Officers deputized special guards, citizens urged the crowd to give up the plan, and it dispersed without harming Reed. Papers reported it as a lynching narrowly checked; Reed was later convicted and sentenced to death.

Reed, described as 'colored' and once a resident of Ceredo, West Virginia, was charged with criminally assaulting Martha Hall, a white girl of eleven or twelve, in October 1902 in Pike county across the river from Matewan. Accounts of his arrest differ: the Big Sandy News placed it at Kenova, while the Ceredo Advance said Constable Mays took him at Brownstown amid 'strong talk of lynching'. At his first trial in the Pike Circuit Court the jury was out twenty hours and could not agree, so Reed remained in the Pikeville jail awaiting retrial.

According to the Pikeville Independent, late on a Sunday afternoon unknown men moved about town and groups gathered near the jail and court house, and it was whispered that Reed would be hanged before morning. By seven o'clock nearly every man in town knew of the plan. Officers hurriedly deputized about three dozen special guards, while several citizens worked quietly to persuade the crowd to drop the plan, and the crowds melted away.

The Independent attributed the failure to the lack of 'an organization or a leader' and expected Reed to be moved to Lexington for safekeeping. A dispatch from Owingsville gave a larger figure of sixty guards placed about the building and said a large crowd had gathered at the jail and court house.

No arrests of anyone in the crowd are reported. At the circuit court term that opened April 27, a second jury found Reed guilty and fixed his punishment at death, and a Courier-Journal special then recalled that his lynching had been 'narrowly averted' at the time of the crime. A state-press comment in the Courier-Journal praised Pike county for letting the law take its course despite 'the gathering of a mob' and said Reed had never had to be removed from the county.

The hanging was set for June 23, and Sheriff Will M. Smith reported that Reed still claimed his innocence. Reed was then granted a new hearing for September, reportedly because the trial judge had received the verdict and discharged the jury on a Sunday. Lynching talk returned with the stay: people came into Pikeville on the original execution date, and a visitor told the Williamson West Virginian that lynching would follow unless the authorities took precautions. No report of the September hearing or of Reed's fate was found.

The episode was reported only in the white press, first by the Big Sandy News of Louisa, which reprinted the Pikeville Independent's account under the headline 'Almost a Lynching'. The Independent called Reed 'the brutal assailant of Little Martha Hall', treated his guilt as settled, and described the crowd's failure as a matter of organization rather than of law. Other Big Sandy News items on the case used headlines such as 'Negro Rapist' and 'Negro Fiend' and called Reed 'the negro ravisher'.

The Courier-Journal condensed the Independent's report into a two-sentence brief saying the jail was guarded on rumors and 'the mob failed to appear,' and a day later ran the Owingsville special under 'Lynchers Frustrated'. That dispatch, which called the prisoner 'Jackson Reed' and warned that 'he may yet be lynched,' reached the Washington Times on March 2 and the Big Stone Gap Post on March 5. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The local account gives about three dozen guards, while the Owingsville dispatch gives sixty and names the prisoner 'Jackson Reed'; the Pikeville Independent, as the local source, is the closer witness. The papers also differ on how far the crowd went: the Independent describes crowds that gathered and melted away, the dispatch an attempt frustrated by guards, and the Courier-Journal's brief a mob that never appeared.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Johnson Reed
bases: Crowds gathered at the Pikeville jail with the reported aim of hanging Johnson Reed, a Black prisoner awaiting retrial, and dispersed after guards were deputized (A4, A6); no one was killed.

No one was killed: the crowd that gathered to hang Reed melted away after about three dozen guards were deputized (A4, A5), so this is an attempted or threatened lynching, not a completed one. The crowd's aim was an unlawful hanging in revenge for an alleged assault on a white girl, but the papers give no number for it (A4, A6).

The Pikeville Independent's local account (A4, condensed in A5) and a separate Owingsville dispatch (A6) both report a crowd at the jail bent on lynching Reed and guards placed to stop it, and the May retrospectives recall threats and a mob (A10, A11); they differ on the number of guards and on whether a mob actually formed (A5).

accounts.gist: Unknown men and groups gathered near the jail on a Sunday evening, it was whispered Reed would be hanged before morning, about three dozen special guards were deputized, citizens urged the plan's abandonment, and the crowds melted away for want of a leader.

accounts.label: Courier-Journal condensation of the Independent
accounts.gist: The jail was guarded by about three dozen special deputies because of rumors of a lynching attempt, and 'the mob failed to appear.'

accounts.label: Owingsville dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob attempted to lynch 'Jackson Reed'; a large crowd gathered at the jail and court house, sixty guards were placed about the building, and the attempt was frustrated.

accounts.label: May retrospectives
accounts.gist: After the conviction, a special dispatch said lynching was 'narrowly averted' at the time of the crime, and a state-press comment praised Pike county for letting the law take its course despite threats and 'the gathering of a mob'.

framing.detail: The Pikeville Independent, quoted under 'Almost a Lynching', called Reed 'the brutal assailant of Little Martha Hall' and regretted nothing but the lack of a leader, while praising the citizens who talked the crowd down.
The Courier-Journal's Owingsville special ran under 'Lynchers Frustrated' and stated as fact that Reed 'assaulted' the girl, adding that 'he may yet be lynched.'
The Washington Times and the Big Stone Gap Post reprinted the Owingsville dispatch with 'it is charged' or 'charged with' and headlines on jail guards checking a mob.
A May state-press comment framed Pike county's restraint as a lesson in law and order to the Bluegrass, while calling Reed 'the wretch'.

record_check.dossier: A Sunday night in February 1903, after the hung jury (reported February 13) and before February 27; most likely February 15 or 22, not fixed by the papers.

Crowds gathered with the stated aim of hanging Reed but made no move on the jail before dispersing; the wire calls it an attempt, while a condensation of the local account says the mob 'failed to appear'. Threatened or attempted is contested.
A gathering near the jail and court house; no assault, siege or demand for the prisoner is reported.
